class_id: a backlog count is read as demand, when most of it is the writer's own historical bugs
feature: any accumulating table nothing consumes — conflicts, failures, queues, alerts, dead letters — whose ROW COUNT is quoted in specs, issues and plans as the size of the problem
symptom: a table that records problems keeps growing because nothing drains it. Its count gets quoted as the size of the work ('2,398 unresolved conflicts, 578 on leadManagers') and features are designed, sized and prioritised from that number. But a table nothing consumes is also a table nobody INSPECTS, so writer bugs that produce meaningless rows accumulate invisibly: a source compared against itself, a comparison where one side is NULL, two values that are byte-identical, or values differing only in punctuation. When the guards for those bugs later land, they stop NEW junk but never remove the OLD rows, so every count taken afterwards still reads the pre-fix world. Universal shape: the count measures how long the writer has been running and how buggy it was, not how much real work exists. The danger is that it is quoted with precision and never re-derived, so a real feature gets designed for a demand that is two orders of magnitude smaller than stated, and its stated first customer may not exist at all.
first_seen: 2026-09-20 -- `data_conflicts` in IPODhan, measured read-only through the sanctioned tunnel on both slots. STAGING: 14,141 unresolved rows, of which 12,774 are a source disagreeing with ITSELF, 1,175 have a NULL on one side, 115 hold byte-identical values and 1 differs only in punctuation -- leaving 76 genuine disagreements, 0.5% of the table. PROD: 2,220 unresolved, 0 same-source (prod is 13 days behind and never ran the code that wrote them), 2,042 null-side, 117 identical, 2 punctuation -- leaving 59 genuine, 2.7%. The spec's §3.1 quoted '31,014 rows, 2,398 unresolved, including all 578 leadManagers conflicts' and the re-read loop (build item 9) was designed and sized around it; measured, leadManagers is 1 genuine row on staging and 2 on prod. The junk classes trace to two writer bugs whose guards landed 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-16: same-source rows stop 2026-08-23 and null-side rows stop 2026-08-24, with zero written after either date, so the guards work and only the historical rows remained. The two slots also disagree in SHAPE, not just size: staging's genuine rows are 38/76 CHITTORGARH-vs-MONEYCONTROL (a retired source, OD-3) while prod's are 43/59 exchange-vs-exchange (BSE-vs-CHITTORGARH 22, CHITTORGARH-vs-NSE 21) with only 5 involving MONEYCONTROL -- so a measurement on one slot does not describe the other
fix_prs: no code fix -- the remedy is a reading discipline plus a cleanup. (1) Before a backlog count is used to size, prioritise or justify a feature, it is DECOMPOSED by the ways the writer can produce a meaningless row, and only the residue is quoted. The decomposition here is four filters and ~40 lines of read-only JavaScript. (2) When a guard lands that stops a junk class, the SAME change plans the removal of the rows already written, or records that it did not -- a guard without a cleanup leaves every future count wrong. (3) A count is re-derived on the slot being discussed; staging and prod differed here by 4x in total and in shape
detection_check: none yet, and one is worth building because this table is the input to a planned feature: a check that reports `data_conflicts` unresolved rows as a DECOMPOSITION (same-source / null-side / identical / normalises-equal / genuine) rather than a single count, run nightly and diffed NEW vs GONE vs SAME per class. That turns the residue into something visible and shrinking rather than a number people quote. The same shape generalises to any nothing-consumes-it table. Note what made this measurable at all: `data_conflicts` stores BOTH values (`value1`, `value2`) plus `resolution_reason`, so the junk classes are derivable from the rows themselves -- a table that stored only 'these disagreed' could not have been decomposed without re-running the writer
